candidates.title: On this day in space! Nov. 24, 1947: The US Navy launches the 1st Aerobee sounding rocket, but it didn't reach space
candidates.raw_excerpt: On Nov. 24, 1947, the U.S. Navy launched the first Aerobee rocket into the sky, but it never reached space. Aerobee was a suborbital sounding rocket designed to study Earth's atmosphere . After World War 2, the United States started reusing erman V-2 rockets for this kind of research. When they started running out of V-2 rockets , the United States constructed its own rockets that were similar but cheaper to build and to launch. In the weeks leading up to the first Aerobee mission, three test flights were launched. Those tests used a dummy version of Aerobee with a live booster to see if the two stages would separate properly. On Aerobee's first real flight, the rocket flew about 35 miles high. That's below the 62-mile (100 kilometers) upper limit for the boundary of space . (NASA and the U.S. military typically consider 50 miles the edge of space.) Mission control cut the flight short after about 30 seconds, because Aerobee started to yaw, and they wanted to keep it from going completely out of control. The first Aerobee sounding rocket launched on Nov. 24, 1947 under a project led by the U.S. Navy. (Image credit: U.S. Navy) Why it mattered Billed as the " most successful sounding rocket of the space age ," the initial Aerobee rocket was suborbital rocket designed to launch experment payload of up to 100 pounds (45 kilograms) to an altitude of 75 miles (121 kilometers) or so. "The Aerobee was designed to carry instruments aloft to collect data on the upper atmosphere and to place small animals in a weightless condition for physiological studies," the U.S. National Museum of the United States Air Force wrote in a mission overview . "It was launched by a solid-propellant booster engine of 18,000 pounds thrust that burned for only two and a half seconds." candidates.raw_excerpt: Last night the White House sent Congress a list of funding it wants included in a new Continuing Resolution (CR) that would keep the government open after the current CR expires on December 11. The request includes $2 billion for NASA’s Artemis program to return astronauts to the Moon and $5 billion for DOD’s Golden Dome missile defense project. CRs keep government departments and agencies funded at their current levels unless Congress specifically includes an exception or “anomaly.” None of the 12 FY2027 appropriations bills have cleared Congress yet and with December 11 fast approaching, Congress must decide whether to pass another CR or face a government shutdown. The image was captured by the European Space Agency's (ESA's) Hera probe, which was sent to rendezvous with Didymos. But more than that, this image reveals incredible details of the Didymos system. Scientists call Didymos a "rubble pile" asteroid , meaning it's a loose body made up of boulders, dust, gravel and other bits of the solar system held together by the asteroid's own gravity. candidates.raw_excerpt:
China and Pakistan will conduct four cooperative scientific experiments aboard China Space Station, involving cyanobacteria, quinoa seeds and two types of composite materials, according to  the Technology and Engineering Center for Space Utilization of Chinese Academy of Sciences.

The Pakistani astronaut on a short-term flight on China Space Station will carry out related experimental operations in orbit.

One of the experiments, proposed by Pakistan’s Space and Upper Atmosphere Research Commission, will examine how cyanobacteria grow and absorb carbon dioxide in space, providing data for future oxygen regeneration and biological production. Cyanobacteria are tiny organisms that use sunlight to grow and release oxygen. The organisms used in the experiment come from Pakistan.

Another experiment, led by the University of Agriculture Faisalabad, will expose 32 quinoa seed samples to the space environment to study their resilience and longevity.

Two materials experiments will test the protective performance of graphene-based composites and the repair efficiency of self-healing carbon fiber composites.

The Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, who will take a short-term flight on China Space Station, will carry out related experimental operations in orbit, according to Chen Mengyun, International Cooperation Project Manager at the Technology and Engineering Center for Space Utilization of Chinese Academy of Sciences.

Chinese and Pakistani scientific teams will also jointly publish papers and share the results of the experiments, said Chen.

The space station will continue to solicit, select and implement new space science projects, Chen said.

She added that China Space Station, also the national space laboratory, is open to scientists worldwide. It solicits proposals for space science and application projects from global scientists on an ongoing basis each year.

candidates.title: UK joins 10 other nations in NATO STARLIFT satellite launch initiative
candidates.raw_excerpt:
The UK has joined 10 other countries in a NATO-led initiative to develop a network of flexible satellite launch services, aiming to ensure more reliable access to space and strengthen security.

The UK Ministry of Defence announced on Sunday that the country had signed the NATO STARLIFT initiative alongside Belgium, Canada, Finland, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden, Türkiye and the Republic of Korea.

STARLIFT aims to work with commercial launch providers and spaceport operators to build a network of launch capabilities across participating countries, making access to space more resilient, responsive and cost-effective.

According to NATO, the initiative will help military users secure launch slots on commercial rockets, including for urgent satellite launches. It will also support improvements to launch infrastructure, logistics and air and maritime traffic management to ensure safe launch operations.

NATO announced the initiative on November 17, following a funding commitment by the participating countries through the NATO Support and Procurement Agency. The agreement was signed in Brussels on October 29.

The UK government said joining STARLIFT supports its updated Space Strategy, published this year, which calls for stronger collective defense through NATO by sharing capabilities, ensuring reliable access to space and improving interoperability among allies. The strategy outlines more than 7.8 billion pounds (about $10.2 billion) in investment to secure the UK's interests and drive growth in the space sector.
